title: How White-collar Crime Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a sponsor read and banter, then cover white-collar crime: a UK/US study of bank robbery payoffs that makes white-collar crime look more lucrative and less risky; a broad definition of white-collar (occupational) crime; types including insider trading, securities fraud, stock touting, antitrust violations, price fixing, bribery, embezzlement, industrial espionage, environmental violations, credit card and bankruptcy fraud; the victim-diffusion problem; history from the 1473 Carrier's case through the Sherman Antitrust Act, Clayton Antitrust Act, muckrakers, E. A. Ross's "criminaloid" concept, and Edwin Sutherland's 1939 coinage of "white collar crime"; the FBI white-collar division (1974), Sarbanes-Oxley (2002) and harsher sentences (Bernie Madoff, Sholam Weiss, Thomas Peters); the difficulty of prosecuting and recovering losses (RICO, Madoff recovery); and bribery abroad under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and Transparency International. The episode closes with a listener mail request about the Electronic Saviors cancer charity compilation and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor read
segments.summary: Hosts open with a sponsor read for Laquais mineral water and banter, then introduce a study of bank robbery economics that concludes white-collar crime pays better and with less risk.

segments.title: Defining white-collar crime
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of defining white-collar crime, describing it as nonviolent crime involving deceit and fraud by someone using their occupation, also called occupational crime.

segments.title: Types of white-collar crime
segments.summary: Examples covered include investment fraud, insider trading, securities fraud and stock manipulation, antitrust violations involving Google and Apple e-book price fixing, bribery, embezzlement as in Office Space, industrial espionage, and environmental violations.

segments.title: Victims and diffuse harm
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how white-collar crimes often lack an identifiable victim, with harm passed along to shareholders, customers, and employees, and debate the sympathy owed to offenders.

segments.title: Carrier's case and early corporate crime
segments.summary: The 1473 Carrier's case, in which a wool carrier kept wool entrusted to him, is described as the origin of a law outlawing an act that was not previously illegal. The hosts then discuss monopolies and the Industrial Revolution.

segments.title: Sherman and Clayton Antitrust Acts
segments.summary: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 is described as vague and weakly enforced, though Standard Oil and American Tobacco were dissolved under it. The Clayton Antitrust Act followed with more specific prohibitions on price discrimination, mergers, interlocking boards, and exclusive contracts. The hosts also discuss big-box retailer practices.

segments.title: Muckrakers, E. A. Ross and Edwin Sutherland
segments.summary: Muckraking journalists exposed corporate abuses, including Upton Sinclair's The Jungle. Sociologist E. A. Ross coined criminaloid, and Edwin Sutherland coined white collar crime in 1939, arguing that the justice system ignored upper-class crime. Critics noted his definition included non-illegal conduct.

segments.title: Modern impacts, FBI division and Sarbanes-Oxley
segments.summary: The hosts discuss ripple effects of corporate fraud on the stock market and public trust, the FBI's white-collar crime division created in 1974, difficulty of detecting white-collar crime, and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 after Enron. They discuss longer sentences for figures such as Bernie Madoff, Sholam Weiss and Thomas Peters, and whether sentences are fair or deterrent.

segments.title: Recovering losses and RICO
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the RICO Act, which allows damages to be claimed up to three times, the difficulty of recovering money, and the Madoff trustee recovering about six billion dollars.

segments.title: International bribery and anti-corruption efforts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss bribery customs abroad, the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and Transparency International's efforts to unify business ethics worldwide.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener requests promotion of the Electronic Saviors compilation fundraising for cancer research, followed by the hosts' sign-off and contact information.
